comparison: Perfect agreement on technical validation (C34-C36). Both evaluations find the BMI approach convincingly validated with appropriate systematic optimization of parameters. OpenEval provides detailed technical assessment while peer review (Reviewer 2) explicitly endorses the validation.

Perfect agreement on delay-performance relationship (C31-C33). Both accept the statistical evidence and validation that the task engages working memory processes. Peer review (Reviewer 3) implicitly accepts this by acknowledging the importance of delay-matched controls.

Strong agreement on main behavioral finding (C37, C40, C24). Both evaluations recognize this as the primary result with dramatic performance improvement on high coherence trials. OpenEval emphasizes within-subject controls while peer reviewers describe it as 'striking' and 'clearly presented.'
Agreement on asymmetric effect (C38-C39). Both accept that low coherence trials don't impair performance relative to random controls. Reviewer 2 explicitly notes this finding without critique.

Agreement on spectral characterization (C42-C47, C107-C111). Both evaluations accept the comprehensive electrophysiological characterization of high coherence states. Peer review notes results are 'clearly presented' with 'appropriate controls and analyses.'
Agreement on temporal persistence (C48). Both accept that coherence effects persist into choice execution phase. These temporal dynamics help address confounds about event-locked coherence.

Agreement on coherence dynamics (C49-C52). Both evaluations accept the autocorrelation and fixed-delay analyses showing coherence fluctuations are not simply anticipatory. Peer reviewers acknowledge these as important controls.

Agreement on unexpected finding but both express uncertainty (C53-C55, C118-C119). OpenEval rates UNCERTAIN due to contradiction with prior work and small sample. Peer reviewers accept the finding as 'robust' but Reviewer 3 identifies it as raising important interpretive questions.

Agreement on mPFC-VMT interactions (C59-C66). Both evaluations accept the three-region recording data showing preferential mPFC-VMT interactions during high coherence. Peer review accepts these as part of mechanistic investigation without challenge.

Perfect agreement on selective spike-LFP effects (C67-C72, C97-C98). Both accept that only a subset of neurons shows modulation without global entrainment changes. Neither evaluation challenges these mechanistic findings.

Partial agreement on VMT entrainment but divergence on interpretation (C73-C75, C120-C121). OpenEval finds robust evidence for VMT-to-mPFC entrainment. Peer reviewers accept the entrainment data but critique the artificial nature of 7 Hz stimulation and note preliminary status (2 animals).

Agreement on complex stimulation effects (C76-C79) but peer review more critical overall. OpenEval documents parameter-dependent effects as well-supported. Peer review (Reviewer 2) describes VMT results as 'inconclusive' due to mixed effects across frequencies.

Divergence on therapeutic implications (C80). OpenEval finds the synthesis appropriately cautious and grounded. Peer review (Reviewer 1) suggests optogenetic inhibition would have been better, questioning the approach's translational value.

Perfect agreement on speculative nature (C83-C89). Both evaluations rate this UNCERTAIN, acknowledging the timescale hypothesis as plausible but untested. Peer review (Reviewer 3) identifies this as a key unresolved question.

Agreement on mechanistic interpretation (C99, C102). Both accept that coherence may reflect communication products rather than scaffolds, consistent with selective neuronal modulation data. Aligns with Reviewer 1's suggestion of alternative mechanisms.

Strong agreement on therapeutic potential (C104-C106). Both evaluations support the translational implications. Editor and reviewers explicitly endorse the importance for brain-machine interface applications and potential for human translation.
Agreement on main conclusions (C29-C30). Both evaluations accept the causal claim justified by prospective BMI design. Peer reviewers describe the main finding as clearly presented and striking.

Divergence on mechanistic model (C90-C96). OpenEval finds anatomical synthesis well-supported and appropriately speculative. Peer review (Reviewer 1) challenges the cortico-thalamo-cortical interpretation, suggesting direct ventral hippocampus-PFC pathway may be primary with VMT passively inheriting theta.

OpenEval evaluates behavioral control analyses (C116-C117) showing shorter BMI delays and reduced IdPhi on low coherence trials. No corresponding peer review evaluation found for these specific control measures.

Minor overlap on theoretical framework (C100-C101). OpenEval synthesizes with prior necessity studies. Peer review engages with alternative mechanisms but focuses more on anatomical pathways than theoretical interpretation of spike-LFP relationships.
